Respite
res'pit
n. (a temporary intermission or delay; the pause Pharaoh used to harden himself, and the seven days Jabesh asked for)
Old French respit, from Latin respectus, a looking back or regard — hence a delay granted. A respite is not a reprieve: the thing is postponed, not cancelled.

Biblical Definition

After the plague of frogs Moses prayed, and the frogs died, and the land stank. “But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said” (Exodus 8:15). The sequence is exact and it recurs through the plague narrative: pressure, promise, relief, hardening. The mercy that removes an affliction is the very thing Pharaoh uses to return to his sin, and the closing clause — as the LORD had said — notes that God had announced this in advance. The other use is a request made in desperation: Nahash the Ammonite had offered Jabesh-gilead terms involving the loss of every right eye, and “the elders of Jabesh said unto him, Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers unto all the coasts of Israel: and then, if there be no man to save us, we will come out to thee” (1 Samuel 11:3). The seven days were granted, Saul heard, and the city was delivered. One respite was used to look for a saviour; the other was used to harden a heart. The pause itself decided nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines respite as a temporary intermission of labor or of any process, an interval of rest, and in law a temporary suspension of the execution of a sentence.

expand to see more

RESPITE, n. Pause; temporary intermission of labor, or of any process or operation; interval of rest.

2. In law, a temporary suspension of the execution of a capital sentence.

3. Delay; forbearance; prolongation of time for the payment of a debt.

REPRIEVE, n. The suspension of the execution of a sentence for a time.

FORBEARANCE, n. The exercise of patience; long suffering; indulgence toward those who injure us.

Key Scripture

Exodus 8:15 — "But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said."

1 Samuel 11:3 — "And the elders of Jabesh said unto him, Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers unto all the coasts of Israel: and then, if there be no man to save us, we will come out to thee."

Nahum 1:3 — "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet."

Romans 3:26 — "To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Delay in judgment is read as evidence that judgment is not coming, and Exodus shows a man drawing exactly that inference and destroying himself with it.

expand to see more

Pharaoh's reasoning in Exodus 8:15 is the reasoning of every age. The frogs are gone; therefore the crisis is over; therefore nothing needs to change. Peter answers the same inference in his own day: scoffers say all things continue as they were from the beginning, and he replies that the Lord is not slack concerning His promise but is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish. The delay is mercy, and it is mercy with a purpose — space to repent. Treating the space as proof that there is nothing to repent of turns the kindest thing God does into the instrument of a man's hardening. Romans 2:4 states it exactly: the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance, and the man who despises it treasures up wrath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Jabesh-gilead did with its seven days. They did not use the respite to negotiate better terms or to persuade themselves the Ammonite was bluffing; they spent it sending messengers to look for a saviour, having already agreed that if none came they would submit. That is the right use of a delay, and it is a fair picture of the interval every hearer of the gospel is living in. The pause is real, it is limited, and its whole value lies in whom one spends it looking for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew revachah, respite or relief — Exodus 8:15, Lamentations 3:56; raphah in the sense of slackening — 1 Samuel 11:3.

expand to see more

Hebrew revachah — a breathing space, relief; Exodus 8:15, and Lamentations 3:56 of a cry for relief.

Hebrew ravach — to be wide, to have room, hence to have relief; the root of the noun.

Hebrew Nahash — the Ammonite king whose terms occasioned the request at Jabesh.

Hebrew Jabesh-gilead — the city Saul delivered, and which later buried his bones with honour.

Romans 2:4 names the danger in the delay: despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering?

Usage

"“When Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart” — mercy turned into an occasion."

"“Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers” — a pause spent looking for a saviour."

"A respite postpones; it does not cancel."
